{{Short description|Branch of logic}}
First-order '''equational [[logic]]''' consists of [[Quantification (logic)|quantifier]]-free terms of ordinary [[first-order logic]], with equality as the only [[predicate symbol]]. The [[model theory]] of this logic was developed into [[universal algebra]] by [[Garrett Birkhoff|Birkhoff]], [[George Grätzer|Grätzer]], and [[Paul Cohn|Cohn]]. It was later made into a branch of [[category theory]] by [[William Lawvere|Lawvere]] ("algebraic theories").<ref>equational logic. (n.d.). The Free On-line Dictionary of Computing. Retrieved October 24, 2011, from Dictionary.com website: http://dictionary.reference.com/browse/equational+logic</ref>
	
The terms of equational logic are built up from variables and constants using function symbols (or operations).

==Syllogism==

Here are the four [[inference rule]]s of logic. <math display="inline">P[x := E]</math> denotes textual substitution of expression <math display="inline">E</math> for variable <math display="inline">x</math> in expression <math display="inline">P</math>. Next, <math display="inline">b = c</math> denotes equality, for <math display="inline">b</math> and <math display="inline">c</math> of the same type, while <math display="inline">b \equiv c</math>, or equivalence, is defined only for <math display="inline">b</math> and <math display="inline">c</math> of type [[Boolean algebra|boolean]]. For <math display="inline">b</math> and <math display="inline">c</math> of type boolean, <math display="inline">b = c</math> and <math display="inline">b \equiv c</math> have the same meaning.

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! scope="row" style="text-align: left" | [[Substitution (logic)|Substitution]]
| If <math display="inline">P</math> is a theorem, then so is <math display="inline">P[x := E]</math>.
| <math display="block">\vdash P \qquad \rightarrow \qquad \vdash P[x := E]</math>
|-
! scope="row" style="text-align: left" | [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]]
| If <math display="inline">P = Q</math> is a theorem, then so is <math display="inline">E[x:= P] = E[x:= Q]</math>.
| <math display="block">\vdash P = Q \qquad \rightarrow \qquad \vdash E[x := P] = E[x := Q]</math>
|-
! scope="row" style="text-align: left" style="text-align: left" | [[Transitive relation|Transitivity]]
| If <math display="inline">P = Q</math> and <math display="inline">Q = R</math> are theorems, then so is <math display="inline">P = R</math>.
| <math display="block">\vdash P = Q, \; \vdash Q = R \qquad \rightarrow \qquad \vdash P = R</math>
|-
! scope="row" style="text-align: left" | Equanimity
| If <math display="inline">P</math> and <math display="inline">P \equiv Q</math> are theorems, then so is <math display="inline">Q</math>.
| <math display="block">\vdash P, \; \vdash P \equiv Q \qquad \rightarrow \qquad \vdash Q</math>
|}

<ref name="gries">Gries, D. (2010). Introduction to equational logic . Retrieved from https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/gries/Logic/Equational.html {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190923093229/http://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/gries/Logic/Equational.html |date=2019-09-23 }}</ref>

==Proof==
We explain how the four inference rules are used in proofs, using the proof of {{clarify span|<math display="inline">\lnot p \equiv p \equiv \bot</math>|reason=Insert parantheses to disambiguate the formula.|date=November 2021}}. The [[List of logic symbols|logic symbols]] <math display="inline">\top</math> and <math display="inline">\bot</math> indicate "true" and "false," respectively, and <math display="inline">\lnot</math> indicates "[[logical negation|not]]." The theorem numbers refer to theorems of ''A Logical Approach to Discrete Math''.<ref name="gries" />

<math display="block">
\begin{array}{lcl}
(0) & & \lnot p \equiv p \equiv \bot \\
(1) & = & \quad \left\langle\; (3.9),\; \lnot(p \equiv q) \equiv \lnot p \equiv q,\; \text{with}\ q := p \;\right\rangle \\
(2) & & \lnot (p \equiv p) \equiv \bot \\
(3) & = & \quad \left\langle\; \text{Identity of}\ \equiv (3.9),\; \text{with}\ q := p \;\right\rangle \\
(4) & & \lnot \top \equiv \bot & (3.8)
\end{array}
</math>

First, lines <math display="inline">(0)</math>&ndash;<math display="inline">(2)</math> show a use of inference rule Leibniz:

<math display="block">
(0) = (2)
</math>

is the conclusion of Leibniz, and its premise <math display="inline">\lnot(p \equiv p) \equiv \lnot p \equiv p</math> is given on line <math display="inline">(1)</math>. In the same way, the equality on lines <math display="inline">(2)</math>&ndash;<math display="inline">(4)</math> are substantiated using Leibniz.

The "hint" on line <math display="inline">(1)</math> is supposed to give a premise of Leibniz, showing what substitution of equals for equals is being used. This premise is theorem <math display="inline">(3.9)</math> with the substitution <math display="inline">p := q</math>, i.e.

<math display="block">
(\lnot(p \equiv q) \equiv \lnot p \equiv q)[p := q]
</math>

This shows how inference rule Substitution is used within hints.

From <math display="inline">(0) = (2)</math> and <math display="inline">(2) = (4)</math>, we conclude by inference rule Transitivity that <math display="inline">(0) = (4)</math>. This shows how Transitivity is used.

Finally, note that line <math display="inline">(4)</math>, <math display="inline">\lnot \top \equiv \bot</math>, is a theorem, as indicated by the hint to its right. Hence, by inference rule Equanimity, we conclude that line <math display="inline">(0)</math> is also a theorem. And <math display="inline">(0)</math> is what we wanted to prove.<ref name="gries" />
